extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. politics, FCC actions, net neutrality, and cybersecurity
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic account of an investigation into a website traffic surge at the Federal Communications Commission, explaining findings about whether the event was a cyberattack and how agency officials responded. Focuses on attribution, agency procedures, and public statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and treat events as cyber security incidents when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The report found "We discovered the FCC had not defined the event internally as a cyber security incident" and that officials had not followed their own cyberattack procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should have an internal definition for cybersecurity incidents and follow established incident-response procedures when applicable; the page specifically notes failing to do so as a procedural lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow required incident-response steps (including contacting DHS CERT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials "had not followed their own cyberattack procedures, including contacting the Department of Homeland Security's Computer Emergency Readiness Team."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an event is treated as a cybersecurity incident, required steps include notifying relevant external responders (e.g., DHS CERT). Failure to perform mandated notifications is a deviation from proper procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use temporal and source correlation for attribution (avoid premature DDoS labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses found "spikes in web traffic coinciding exactly with the timing of: (1) the release of information during the ... episode; (2) the release of the episode on The Last Week Tonight with John Oliver YouTube channel; and (3) tweets about that release."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation of traffic spikes with public broadcasts and social-media activity can indicate organic, audience-driven surges rather than coordinated external attacks; investigators should consider such correlations before characterizing events as distributed denial-of-service attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between actors' intent and impact on commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: The report and FCC statement noted that "These actors were not attempting to file comments themselves; rather they made it difficult for legitimate commenters to access and file with the FCC."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should separate whether traffic was intentionally malicious (attempting to file comments or manipulate the system) from whether the practical outcome was to disrupt legitimate public participation; both intent and impact matter for understanding and responding to incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accuracy and transparency in public statements about incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC issued a news release describing the incident as an attack, and the chairman criticized the former CIO for providing "inaccurate information about this incident to me, my office, Congress, and the American people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency communications to the public and Congress should be accurate and not prematurely politicized; inaccurate characterizations of incidents can prompt oversight and undermine trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that large publicity events can cause massive traffic spikes
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation ties the surge to John Oliver urging viewers to comment; within minutes traffic "spiked by 3,116%", "resulting in the disruption of system availability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational planning for public comment systems should anticipate that media-driven calls-to-action (TV segments, YouTube posts, tweets) can create extremely large, sudden traffic loads that impair availability even absent malicious intent.
